posts.title: AI Is Making Me Better at My Job. But Will I Have One in Five Years?
posts.excerpt: AI is making me more productive every day, but it also raises an uncomfortable question: what happens when the skills that built our careers are no longer enough to sustain them?
posts.body:
I've been using AI almost every day since I started working. Writing emails, preparing documentation, writing code, debugging errors, solving problems, and doing things that would otherwise take hours. It has become a regular part of how I work.

Honestly, I cannot imagine going back to the way I used to work before.

But there's something interesting about this experience. The better AI gets at helping me do my job, the more I find myself thinking about whether that job will even exist in its current form five years from now.

And I don't think I'm the only one thinking about this.

## The strange feeling of becoming more productive

I don't come from an engineering background. I understand programming logic and can work with data, but I'm not someone who can sit down and write thousands of lines of complex code from scratch.

Yet today, I can use AI to build things, solve technical problems, debug errors, and understand concepts that would have required significantly more time and expertise earlier.

Sometimes, I look at the output and genuinely wonder how far we've come.

Think about what this means. Someone who previously couldn't perform a particular task independently can now do it with the help of AI. The barrier to entry for several technical activities is getting lower.

That's exciting. It allows people to experiment, build things, and solve problems they might never have attempted otherwise.

But there's another side to it.

If I can do more work in less time, and someone else can do the same, companies might eventually need fewer people to produce the same output.

The work doesn't necessarily disappear. The number of people required to do it might.

## What happens when ten people become two?

I think this is one of the more important questions we need to ask about AI.

We often discuss job replacement as if a company will suddenly fire everyone and let AI run the entire business. That's one possibility in some roles, but the transition could be much less dramatic.

Imagine a team of ten people working on a project. AI tools improve their productivity to the point where two people can now deliver the same output.

The company has a choice. It could use those productivity gains to build more products, take on more projects, and expand its business. Or it could maintain the same output with a smaller team.

Both outcomes are possible. And the decision will depend on business demand, costs, competition, and what the company wants to achieve.

The uncomfortable part is that even if the overall economy grows, there is no guarantee that every worker benefits from that growth.

We could become significantly more productive as a society while some people struggle to find work.

And that's where my excitement about AI starts mixing with uncertainty.

## What if everyone starts building instead?

There's another possibility that I find equally interesting.

What if AI doesn't just reduce the number of people needed to build things? What if it dramatically increases the number of things we can build?

Think about how many ideas never become businesses because people lack the technical skills, money, or resources to execute them.

Someone might understand a problem in their industry but have no idea how to build software to solve it. Another person might have a great product idea but cannot afford to hire a development team.

AI could change that equation.

A smaller team, or even an individual, might be able to build products that previously required an entire organisation. Starting a business could become cheaper, experimentation could become faster, and more niche problems could become commercially viable.

Perhaps we'll eventually see millions of small businesses and independent creators building products for specific audiences.

Instead of a handful of large companies employing thousands of people each, we might see a much more distributed economy, with smaller teams creating a wider variety of products and services.

I find that possibility genuinely exciting.

But I also think we need to be careful not to assume that new opportunities will automatically compensate for every job lost.

The jobs created might require different skills, exist in different locations, or offer completely different compensation. Someone whose career has been built around a particular profession cannot necessarily transition overnight into running an AI-powered business.

The transition matters just as much as the destination.

## Is learning one skill still enough?

For a long time, the formula seemed relatively straightforward. Pick a field, acquire specialised skills, gain experience, and build a career around them.

That approach still has value. Deep expertise isn't suddenly becoming irrelevant.

But I'm increasingly questioning whether relying entirely on one skill, one job, or one source of income is a sensible long-term strategy in a world where technology can change the value of certain skills so quickly.

Something you've spent years mastering could become easier for others to do with AI. That doesn't necessarily make your experience worthless, but it could change what employers are willing to pay for it.

Perhaps the advantage will increasingly belong to people who can combine domain knowledge, problem-solving, judgement, communication, and the ability to use new tools effectively.

The specific tools will change. The ability to learn and adapt may matter much longer.

For me, this also means exploring things beyond my regular job, experimenting with AI tools, and trying to build products of my own. Not because I know exactly what the future holds, but because I don't.

I would rather experiment while I have the opportunity than wait until circumstances force me to.

## We are still figuring this out

I'm genuinely excited about what AI could make possible. There are problems we might solve, businesses we might create, and opportunities we haven't even imagined yet.

At the same time, I don't think we should dismiss the possibility of a painful restructuring of the labour market. Productivity gains and economic growth do not automatically translate into security for every individual.

Maybe we'll end up working fewer hours, building more businesses, and having access to opportunities that are difficult to imagine today.

Or maybe the transition will be far more disruptive than we expect.

I don't have a definitive answer, and I don't think anyone can confidently predict exactly how this will unfold.

But one thing is becoming clear to me: the question is no longer just how AI can help us do our jobs better.

It's also what happens when AI changes what those jobs are worth, how many people are needed to do them, and what it takes to build a career in the first place.

I'm excited to be part of this transition. I'm just not entirely sure where it will take us.

And perhaps that's precisely why we need to keep learning, experimenting, and adapting.

posts.title: The Great Dumb-Down and the Ultimate Career Hack No One Is Talking About
posts.excerpt: AI is making execution easier for everyone. The real career advantage may now lie elsewhere: deep expertise, first-principles thinking, curiosity, and the ability to truly understand what you are doing.
posts.body:
Let’s be honest for a second. Look around at what’s happened over the last three to four years. AI is everywhere. Corporate offices are putting massive pressure on everyone to "utilize AI," squeeze out some ROI, and automate everything in sight. There is an expectation now that no matter what your job is, you can just turn to an LLM and get it done.

Even if you didn’t know how to do something yesterday, you can prompt your way through it today. It makes things simpler, sure. But step back and look at what it’s actually doing to us.

## The Execution Trap

People have started becoming dumber.

Think about how we used to work. Back in the day, if you wanted to write code, you had to learn syntax. You had to sit down, stare at a bug, reason things out, and actually think through the logic. You built mental models.

Now? We are increasingly becoming execution-oriented. People throw a prompt at a machine, copy the output, and call it a day. The actual process of thinking can be bypassed because companies primarily care about one thing: the output.

And if this continues—and let’s face it, it’s only accelerating—people risk losing their cognitive edge over time. I see it happening right in the office. People use an LLM to knock out a task in five seconds, and what do they do with the rest of their time? They aren’t necessarily learning or reflecting. They are often doom-scrolling on their phones. Social media has trained us to stay busy staring at a screen while the machine does the actual heavy lifting.

## When Everyone Has AI, No One Does

Here is the big realization we need to have: **if AI is in the hands of everyone, execution is no longer a competitive advantage.**

If anyone can write an email, draft a piece of code, or analyze a spreadsheet in three seconds just by typing a prompt, then doing those things doesn’t make you special anymore. The playing field hasn’t just leveled; it has been flattened.

So, what happens next? Who are the people who are going to lead in this new era?

It’s probably not going to be the people who are simply the fastest prompt writers or the best at finding quick fixes. The people who stand out will be the ones going back to the absolute basics: **genuine subject-matter expertise, deep research, and first-principles thinking.**

## Your Real Opportunity Right Now

Ironically, this hyper-driven AI boom may be one of the best opportunities for anyone willing to step back and do the hard work.

While a massive number of people are distracted—letting machines execute tasks while their own attention gets consumed by endless feeds—you have a golden window to build a real, difficult-to-copy edge.

Instead of spending all day letting an LLM do your thinking, use the time it saves to actually learn. Pick up books. Dive into academic research. Understand why things work under the hood, not just how to get a script to run. Go back to first principles.

In a world full of fast executors who don’t always understand what they are shipping, the person with deep, fundamental knowledge can stand out like a lighthouse.

## The Ultimate Differentiator

AI can mimic a lot of things, but genuine comprehension is different. When everyone has access to powerful AI tools, simply knowing how to use the tools becomes less differentiated. What matters more is the **depth of understanding you bring to the interaction.**

So don’t fall into the trap of outsourcing your mind entirely. Let the machine handle the grunt work, but protect your curiosity. Read the deep stuff. Master your domain. Understand the fundamentals. Question the output. Build an intellect that can’t simply be copy-pasted.

That may be one of the biggest career advantages of the AI era: **use AI to accelerate your execution, while deliberately investing the time it saves into becoming someone who actually understands.**

That’s how you build an edge in the next era.

posts.title: Beyond the Founder Title: The Reality of Building
posts.excerpt: We fell in love with the idea of becoming founders, but forgot what it takes to build something real. Success may look overnight, but it often takes a decade of work, patience, and belief.
posts.body:
Over the last five to seven years, especially since 2017–18, we have seen a massive rise in startups in India. With companies reaching billion-dollar valuations, the words *founder* and *co-founder* became much more mainstream. Suddenly, everyone seemed fascinated by the idea of building a company, raising money, becoming successful, and having something of their own.

And honestly, I was one of those people, too.

I wanted to become a founder or co-founder. There was something fascinating about building a company, creating a product, or starting something from scratch and being able to say, "I built this." Having your name associated with something you created felt like an achievement in itself.

But somewhere in all this fascination, I think we missed something important.

We became so obsessed with the idea of becoming successful that we forgot what it actually takes to get there.

## We Saw the Valuations, But Not the Years Behind Them

Think about companies like Zerodha, Zomato, and Delhivery. Today, they are well-known businesses, and their founders are often celebrated for what they have built. But these companies didn't become what they are today overnight.

There were years of work behind them. Years of figuring things out, making mistakes, trying different approaches, dealing with uncertainty, and finding ways to keep going.

There must have been days when things weren't working. Days when money was tight, growth was slower than expected, or the founders themselves probably wondered whether they were building something that would eventually work.

That's the part of the story we don't see as often.

We see the funding announcements, the billion-dollar valuations, the interviews, the podcasts, and the success stories. We see founders talking about their journeys after they have already achieved something significant.

What we don't always see is the decade of work that made those conversations possible.

And when you're a student or a young professional looking at all this, it's easy to develop the impression that starting a company is a shortcut to success. You start something, raise funding, become popular, and eventually make a lot of money.

Of course, nobody would describe it that simply if you asked them directly. But the image of entrepreneurship that we consume can sometimes make it feel that way.

For a while, I think I was attracted to that image, too. I wanted to build something, be known for it, and achieve something significant in life. There is nothing inherently wrong with wanting any of those things. But over time, I started looking at the whole idea differently.

## The Problem With Wanting an Overnight Success

We all love overnight success stories.

Someone builds a company, launches a product, or starts sharing their work, and suddenly, it seems like everything changes for them. They become successful, their work reaches millions of people, and their life looks completely different.

But here's the thing about overnight success: it often comes after years of work that nobody was paying attention to.

You might work on something for five years, seven years, or even ten years before it finally takes off. And when it does, people might describe it as an overnight success because they only noticed you when things started working.

That doesn't mean every startup needs ten years to succeed. Some businesses grow quickly, and some ideas find a market much sooner than expected. Others take much longer, and plenty never work out at all.

The point is that you cannot build your entire approach around the expectation that things will happen quickly.

I've had the opportunity to speak with a few founders who have built companies worth millions, and even billions, of dollars. One thing that stood out to me was how deeply hard work seemed to be ingrained in them.

I'm talking about people who worked 16 or 18 hours a day in their early years, and whose instinct was to keep solving problems, looking at situations from different angles, and figuring out what needed to be done next.

It wasn't simply about putting in long hours. It was about developing a certain way of thinking.

They would encounter a problem, try to understand it, look for a solution, and keep moving. Their attention was on getting things done rather than constantly thinking about how successful they might eventually become.

And I highly doubt that every founder who built a successful company started with the certainty that they were going to create a billion-dollar business.

Sometimes, you start with a problem you want to solve. You build something, learn from the people using it, make changes, and keep going. Eventually, that thing might become much bigger than you initially imagined.

But you cannot predict that outcome at the beginning.

## You Need to Be Comfortable With Not Knowing

I think this is one of the most important things to understand if you want to build something of your own.

You might have an idea today, but you don't know whether it will work. You don't know whether people will pay for it, whether the market is large enough, or whether someone else will solve the same problem better than you.

And that's okay.

You don't necessarily need to have your billion-dollar idea figured out at 22, 25, or 30. You don't need to put yourself under pressure to build a successful startup within the next two years just because everyone around you seems to be doing something exciting.

You can have a job and learn from the work you're doing. You can observe how businesses operate, understand the problems people face, start small side projects, and talk to people working in different industries.

You can build something, realise it isn't working, and start again.

Every project teaches you something. Every conversation gives you a different perspective. And every problem you encounter gives you an opportunity to understand the world a little better.

Over time, you might come across a problem that genuinely interests you, one that you understand well enough to do something about. You might find a group of people who need a solution, or notice an opportunity that others haven't paid much attention to.

Perhaps that's when you find something worth building.

And even then, you won't necessarily know where it will lead.

You could build a small business that generates a comfortable income. You could create a product that serves thousands of people. Or you could build something that eventually becomes much larger than you ever imagined.

There is no guarantee. But the process of learning, experimenting, and building puts you in a much better position than simply waiting for the perfect idea to arrive.

## India Has Enormous Opportunities. We Just Need Patience.

I genuinely believe the enthusiasm around startups in India is a good thing.

We have an enormous population, a tremendous amount of diversity, and people dealing with very different problems across regions, industries, and income groups. There are opportunities to build products and services for communities that existing businesses may not be serving well enough.

And we're still far from solving all the problems that exist around us.

Even with AI becoming increasingly capable, I believe there will be decades of opportunities to build useful products, improve existing systems, and solve problems that matter to people.

We talk a lot about an eventual era of abundance, where technology makes goods and services significantly cheaper and more accessible. It's an exciting possibility, although I still wonder what abundance really means in an economic sense. Resources are finite, human needs evolve, and making something cheaper doesn't necessarily mean every problem disappears.

But we don't need to resolve those questions today to recognise how much remains to be done.

There is still so much to build.

What matters is approaching these opportunities with the right expectations. The goal shouldn't simply be to become a founder because the title sounds exciting. It should be to find something worth working on and commit yourself to making it better.

The title might come later. It might never come. But the work itself can still be meaningful.

## Build, Believe, and Give It Time

Over the last few years, my own thinking about this has changed.

I'm still interested in building something of my own. That hasn't gone away. But I'm less interested in the idea of becoming a founder just for the sake of being called one.

Instead, I've started paying more attention to the things around me. The work I do, the problems I encounter, the things happening in the world, and the conversations I have with people.

I'm interested in learning about different fields, experimenting with side projects, and understanding where there might be an opportunity to create something useful.

I don't have everything figured out, and I don't think I need to.

Maybe something I work on will turn into a business in a year. Maybe it will take a decade. Maybe the first few things I try won't work at all. I can live with that, provided I'm learning, improving, and continuing to do the work.

Because ultimately, building something requires more than enthusiasm. It requires patience, a strong work ethic, the willingness to deal with uncertainty, and the ability to keep going when the results aren't immediately visible.

And, at least for me, it also requires belief.

Not the kind of belief where you convince yourself that everything will magically work out. Rather, the belief that you can keep learning, become better at what you do, figure things out along the way, and give yourself a genuine chance of succeeding.

You don't know when things will click. You don't know which project will lead somewhere or which conversation will change how you think. But you can keep putting yourself in situations where those possibilities exist.

And maybe, after years of working on something, there will be a moment when everything starts coming together. From the outside, it might look like an overnight success.

You'll know how much came before it.

So, if you want to build something of your own, go ahead. Start experimenting. Build small things. Talk to people. Learn about problems that interest you. Take your work seriously.

But don't put yourself under unnecessary pressure to make it big within a particular timeline.

You don't need to become a founder tomorrow. You don't need a billion-dollar idea today. And you certainly don't need to have your entire life figured out before you begin.

**You just need to start doing the work, stay patient enough to keep learning, and believe that you can build something worthwhile over time.**

The opportunity might take a year to appear, or it might take ten.

You cannot control the timeline. But you can control whether you're doing the work that gives you a chance.
